items.followUp: Explain the formation of a double covalent bond in an oxygen molecule.

rubric.why: The definition must identify mutual sharing of electron pairs as the basis of a covalent bond.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as a bond formed by sharing electron pairs between atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential idea of sharing electron pair(s) between atoms.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one pair of electrons is shared.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two pairs of electrons are shared.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond involves three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that three pairs of electrons are shared.

rubric.why: Suitable examples show the different types of covalent bond.
rubric.description: Gives examples, such as H₂ for a single bond, O₂ for a double bond, and N₂ for a triple bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for appropriate examples representing the bond types.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms mutually share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons; for example, N₂.

items.followUp: Define chemical properties and give one example.

rubric.why: Physical properties are identified by observation or measurement.
rubric.description: States that physical properties can be observed or measured.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for saying that they are observed or measured.

rubric.why: The defining feature is that measuring or observing the property does not change the substance's chemical composition.
rubric.description: States that determining a physical property does not change the substance chemically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-chemical-change idea.

modelAnswer: Physical properties are characteristics of a substance that can be observed or measured without changing its chemical composition.

items.followUp: Calculate the number of moles in 24.0 g of carbon.

rubric.why: The number of moles is calculated by dividing mass by molar mass.
rubric.description: Uses the relation n = m/M and the molar mass of carbon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relation and/or appropriate carbon molar mass.

rubric.why: 9.0 g of carbon corresponds to 9.0/12.0 = 0.75 mol.
rubric.description: Gives the calculated number of moles with the unit.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 9.0 g = 0.0090 kg; M(C) = 12.0 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0120 kg mol⁻¹.

items.followUp: Define biochemistry and name two substances studied in this branch.

rubric.why: Biochemistry concerns the chemical substances and processes associated with living things.
rubric.description: Identifies the study of chemical substances or processes in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chemistry with living organisms.

rubric.why: Examples of biochemical subject matter demonstrate the scope of the field.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a topic within biochemistry, such as biomolecules or metabolic processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example or application.

modelAnswer: Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies the chemical substances and processes occurring in living organisms.
Its scope includes substances such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats and nucleic acids, and the chemical reactions and metabolism of living organisms.

items.followUp: How can a radioactive isotope be used to examine the thyroid gland?

rubric.why: Radioactive iodine is taken up by the thyroid and can be used to examine its function.
rubric.description: Identifies radioactive iodine, such as iodine-131, as the tracer used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming radioactive iodine or a suitable iodine radioisotope.

rubric.why: The uptake or distribution of the tracer is detected to assess the thyroid.
rubric.description: Explains that thyroid uptake is traced or measured with a detector or scan.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining how the tracer is detected or used to examine the gland.

modelAnswer: Goitre can be investigated using radioactive iodine, such as iodine-131, which is taken up by the thyroid gland.
The uptake and distribution of the radioactive iodine are detected with a suitable detector or thyroid scan.

items.followUp: Describe how atomic size changes across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Across a period, electronegativity generally rises from left to right.
rubric.description: States that electronegativity increases across a period from left to right.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction across a period.

rubric.why: Down a group, electronegativity generally falls.
rubric.description: States that electronegativity decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction down a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, electronegativity generally increases from left to right.
Down a group, electronegativity generally decreases from top to bottom.

items.followUp: State how atomic radius changes across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Shielding effect increases down a group as additional electron shells are added.
rubric.description: States that shielding effect increases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct trend down a group.

rubric.why: Across a period, electrons are added to the same main shell, so shielding is approximately constant.
rubric.description: States that shielding effect remains approximately constant across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct trend across a period.

modelAnswer: Down a group, shielding effect increases because the number of occupied electron shells increases.
Across a period, shielding effect remains nearly constant because added electrons enter the same shell.

items.followUp: State the number of electrons in the stable outer shell represented by the duplet and octet rules.

rubric.why: A duplet is a stable arrangement of two electrons in the outer shell.
rubric.description: States that the duplet rule involves two outer-shell electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the two-electron arrangement.

rubric.why: An octet is a stable arrangement of eight electrons in the outer shell.
rubric.description: States that the octet rule involves eight outer-shell electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the eight-electron arrangement.

modelAnswer: According to the duplet rule, an atom becomes stable when its outermost shell contains two electrons.
According to the octet rule, an atom becomes stable when its outermost shell contains eight electrons.
